1) Outcome: the bomb exploded due to time running out. I contributed by inspecting the module and attempting the instructed cut; you contributed by interpreting the manual and giving cut instructions and requesting bomb-edge info. We lost time after the strike and during the later full-side search.
2) Communication challenges: I initially described the wire panel in a way that sounded non-standard (I said there were no terminals/cut points), which led you to doubt the module type and gave an incorrect instruction path. Also, I didn’t provide a complete bomb-edge survey (ports/batteries/indicators) early, so later we had to spend time rotating/rolling while the timer kept draining.
3) Mistakes/missed opportunities: My biggest mistake was not zooming in immediately and carefully confirming whether wires had visible endpoints/terminals before reporting; the later zoom-in showed cut points existed, meaning my first description was incomplete. Your cut instruction (wire 2) produced a strike (one red X appeared), indicating either the rule set didn’t apply (wrong module assumptions) or earlier info was still mismatched. We could have avoided this by first confirming: exact wire colors, exact count, presence of a serial odd/even last digit, and any special module features (e.g., a star/LED per wire if it wasn’t the simple wires module). Another missed opportunity was not prioritizing a fast, systematic edge check at the very start.
4) What worked well: When we re-checked, we did tighten the description (wire order and colors, confirmation that 2 was cut, strike feedback). What didn’t work: acting on an instruction before we were fully aligned on what module it was and before collecting global bomb info that many rules depend on.
5) If we played again: I’d immediately do a full bomb survey first (serial, batteries, indicators, ports) before touching any module. For each module, I’d always zoom in first, then describe every interactive element and any per-wire symbols/LEDs, and I’d explicitly confirm “this appears cuttable / has terminals” before you apply a manual rule. After any strike, we’d pause and re-validate assumptions rather than continue with the same rule set.
6) Lessons: In collaborative puzzles, early shared context (serial/ports/batteries) prevents later thrashing. Also, precise visual confirmation beats inference—especially when a module “looks like” something but has extra features. Finally, we should treat a strike as evidence of a model mismatch and immediately switch to verification mode rather than incremental guessing.
